A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same projection-based model-editing work, renamed from DeTox to ProFS. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, and their methods, equations, figures and tables can be matched despite reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original toxicity and capability evaluations across five models, comparisons with DPO, ablations, robustness experiments and layer-attribution analyses.

after.justification: v4 retains these original experiments and adds detoxification-baseline comparisons, broader preference-alignment results and qualitative case studies.

M1.justification: Section 4 and Algorithm 1 retain the same embedding differences, corpus-mean projection, top-k singular-vector selection and MLP-weight projection. DeTox becomes ProFS; applying the procedure to broader preferences does not introduce a documented algorithmic adaptation.

E1.justification: v4 adds alignment on HH-Golden and PKU-SafeRLHF, including 19 preference categories beyond toxicity, such as privacy violations and economic crime. The original toxicity data, RealToxicityPrompts evaluation and seven capability tasks remain. This substantially expands the evaluated task coverage.

E2.justification: v1 principally compares the proposed method with DPO and unedited models. v4 Tables 3 and 13 additionally evaluate DExperts and Toxification Reversal, extending comparisons to decoding-based and attention-activation editing methods. Other newly discussed methods are not reported as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New protocols include GPT-4o mini scoring and win rates, with both methods using 500 HH-Golden training examples, and GPT2-XL perplexity of generated responses for the detoxification comparison. Appendix F.2 introduces method-specific noise interventions: label flips, expert/anti-expert swaps and positive/negative prompt swaps. The retained toxicity experiment settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v4 adds robustness stress tests for DExperts and Toxification Reversal, singular-vector interpretation at another layer, and two before/after response case studies. It also reports 93.2% judge agreement with training preference labels. Existing centering, sample-selection, sample-size, layer-selection and additivity analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions specify three randomly sampled runs with means and standard deviations, and retain the ten-draw random-gradient comparison. v4 introduces no new stated uncertainty-estimation or significance-testing procedure. Its added preference win rates are presented as point estimates without accompanying uncertainty.

E6.justification: The original Table 2 and matched ablation/capability results are unchanged. v4 adds DExperts and Toxification Reversal toxicity scores of 13.87% and 27.94%, HH-Golden win rates of 78.2% for ProFS versus 74.1% for DPO, and PKU-SafeRLHF win rates ranging from 0.56 to 0.88. These are new comparisons. The new baseline tables also list DPO toxicity as 36.26%, while retained Table 2 still reports 36.36%, without explaining the difference.

T1.justification: v4 removes the explicit transformer/MLP mapping and matrix-dimension definitions from v1 Section 3, Equation 1, retaining a short verbal key/value description. The substantive factor-model assumptions, subspace-recovery bound, label-noise argument and DPO-gradient derivation remain unchanged; the denoising appendix is relocated to B.4.

C1.justification: The central claims of sample-efficient, noise-robust weight editing and a denoised first-step DPO connection remain. v4 additionally claims effectiveness for alignment across multiple preferences in Section 7 and Appendix H. The new title foregrounds the DPO connection already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: v4 removes v1 Section 9's caution that subtle preferences may be difficult because their subspaces overlap with desired context. It instead interprets the new preference experiments as evidence of broader applicability and the expanded baseline tests as showing uniquely combined robustness and efficiency. The singular-vector-selection and MLP-only limitations remain.

D1.justification: v4 supplies the complete GPT-4o mini judging prompt, access information and metadata for the added preference datasets, and scoring and perturbation instructions for the new comparisons. Existing editing and LoRA settings, hardware, timing information and code-access statement remain substantially unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds a substantial detoxification literature discussion covering tuning, decoding and editing approaches. It positions the MLP analysis as complementary to Toxification Reversal's attention-head analysis and adds relevant works such as DExperts, GeDi and detoxification through knowledge editing. The earlier extended task-vector discussion and some associated citations are removed.

P1.justification: Beyond renaming the paper and method, v4 rewrites and reorganizes related work and preliminaries, revises rank-selection and layer-attribution explanations, restructures the appendices around robustness, mechanisms and broader preferences, and removes the NeurIPS checklist. Much of the core method and theoretical exposition remains recognizable.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn with colored subspaces and a clearer weight-editing diagram. New comparison, preference-result, example and judge-prompt tables expand the presentation; existing tables are reordered and relocated, and document styling changes throughout. Figure 3 reverses its curve colors while retaining the old color description in its caption.

improvement.justification: v4 makes the evaluation more informative by adding relevant detoxification competitors and their fluency tradeoffs, plus initial evidence beyond toxicity with a disclosed judging prompt. These gains are limited by unspecified evaluation sample counts and missing uncertainty for the new win rates, non-equivalent noise interventions across baselines, and removal of the earlier subtle-preference caveat. The revision broadens the evidence without substantially resolving its reliability limitations.
